title: On the Salience of Low-Probability Tokens for AI-Generated Text Detection: A Multiscale Uncertainty Perspective
claim: Statistical detectors fail in two ways: shared boilerplate swamps discriminative signal, and single-score estimates flip under small perturbations.
layout: 2 rounded panels side by side, left-to-right flow, red perturbation lightning bolt
description: Two rounded panels, each titled with a challenge. The left panel, 'Boilerplate Dominance', shows a human avatar with a speech bubble containing a sentence in blue and orange text. An arrow leads to a bar chart of conditional token probabilities. Tall blue bars are boilerplate and short orange bars are informative low-probability tokens. A solid blue mean line μ sits above a dashed red threshold τ. Another arrow leads to a gray detector box that reads 'μ > τ' and a red 'Predicted as AI' label with an X, marking a misclassification. The right panel, 'Brittle Point Estimates', stacks two robot-icon rows. A red 'perturbation' lightning arrow links them. Each row has a dotted-border line plot of token probabilities. The lower plot shows a 'Prob Drop' with a red dot and arrow, so μ < τ and the prediction flips from AI to human, marked with a red X.
caption: Two challenges faced by statistical methods which use proxy model to score. Left: Boilerplate dominance. Sequencelevel aggregation of token-wise conditional probabilities can be dominated by high-probability boilerplate spans that are common to both human and LLM writing, leading to misclassification (e.g., a human-written sentence predicted as AI-generated when the average score µ exceeds a threshold τ). Right: Brittle point estimates. Collapsing each conditional distribution to a single probability score discards distributional shape, making decisions sensitive to surface-level perturbations (e.g., decoding or paraphrasing), which can substantially shift µ and flip the prediction.
abstract: AI-generated text increasingly blends with human writing, raising practical risks such as misinformation, academic misuse, and corpora contamination. While statistical detectors are appealing for efficiency and generalization, they suffer from two key limitations. (i) Boilerplate dominance, boilerplate tokens shared across human and LLM writing can overwhelm discriminative signals. (ii) Brittle point estimates, relying on a single probability score yields unstable decisions under adversarial manipulations. To address these issues, we propose Uncertainty, a multiscale uncertainty estimator that focuses on informative low-probability tokens, which more clearly expose distributional discrepancies. Locally, it alleviates boilerplate dominance by averaging the log-probabilities of low-probability tokens; globally, it reduces brittleness by capturing the distributional shape of this low-probability region via RÃ©nyi entropy. We further extend the detector to Uncertainty++ via conditional independent sampling, yielding a more stable uncertainty estimation. Experiments across seven datasets and sixteen LLMs demonstrate high effectiveness, generalization, and robustness. Our code is available at https://github.com/guoyikai2000/Uncertainty-AIGT.
